strengths: Addresses a practical bottleneck in multi-step image editing by reusing successful tool sequences and retaining search as a fallback.
The fast/slow architecture is intuitive, interpretable, and potentially useful: symbolic activation rules expose when each learned subroutine should apply.
Reports promising efficiency-quality trade-offs on 121 complex tasks, including 1–8-step instructions, and includes relevant ablations for fallback search and subroutine verification.
The appendix provides prompts, algorithms, the learned rule table, evaluation criteria, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The evaluation has serious test-contamination risk: subroutine changes are repeatedly validated on new prompts constructed from the same 121 base images later used for the main benchmark. Thus the benchmark is not fully held out despite claims of generalization.

The headline 49.3% cost reduction compares FaSTA* at 29.5 seconds against the original 58.2-second CoSTA* configuration. The paper's own matched single-chain CoSTA* baseline costs 46.8 seconds, reducing the attributable improvement to about 37%; this distinction is not reflected in the central claim.

Reported execution cost does not clearly account for OpenAI o1 induction, LLM/VLM calls, or the expensive repeated validation of every proposed rule on 20–25 tasks with retries. Without total or amortized system cost and a break-even analysis, the central cost-efficiency claim is incomplete.

Human evaluation lacks essential information such as the number and recruitment of raters, blinding, independent judgments, aggregation, inter-rater agreement, and uncertainty estimates. No statistical tests or repeated-run variability support the small quality differences.

The learning data are described only as unspecified random images and newly created prompts, and code/resources are not clearly supplied. Model versions, decoding settings, thresholds, sampling seeds, and the resolution of multiple eligible subroutines are insufficiently specified for reproducibility.

External generalization is supported only by a few selected MagicBrush examples rather than a quantitative evaluation. The principal experiment uses a small benchmark inherited from the closest prior work, while most non-primary baseline numbers are copied from that work rather than freshly controlled comparisons.

Technical novelty is moderate: mining reusable tool macros and falling back to search is natural, while positioning the method as a novel form of in-context reinforcement learning is insufficiently justified and weakly connected to prior work on options, skills, program induction, caching, and case-based planning.

There are presentation and consistency issues, including an unrelated 'Bi-Directional Block Self-Attention' phrase in the method, duplicate CoSTA* references, an undefined output variable in the execution algorithm, and several grammatical errors. The paper also omits discussion of misuse and other risks specific to automated image editing.

strengths: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/e540131baf9c417fa9d9c8df95a3995d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a practical bottleneck in tool-using image-editing agents: avoiding repeated search for recurring tool sequences.

The fast-subroutine/slow-search fallback is intuitive and potentially useful: common cases receive inexpensive cached plans, while local A* search can recover when a rule is unavailable or fails a quality check.
The paper provides useful implementation detail, including the complete learned rule table, algorithms, prompts, qualitative examples, and ablations of verification and fallback.
The reported results suggest a promising efficiency-quality trade-off: FaSTA* attains 0.91 reported quality versus 0.94 for CoSTA*, while reducing measured execution time.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is not genuinely held out. Although the traces used to propose rules reportedly come from external tasks, every proposed rule is accepted or rejected using subtask-specific datasets built from the same 121 base images as the main CoSTA* benchmark. This allows the final rule library to adapt repeatedly to the test-image distribution, substantially weakening the generalization claim.

The advertised 49.3% saving conflates two changes. CoSTA* takes 58.2 seconds with its original tree prompt but only 46.8 seconds with the paper's new chain prompt; FaSTA* takes 29.5 seconds. Thus a sizeable part of the headline gain comes from prompt simplification, while the isolated subroutine benefit against the matched chain-based baseline is approximately 37%, not 49.3%.

The cost accounting is incomplete. Reported execution time appears to omit or at least does not separately quantify LLM/VLM calls for context extraction and subroutine selection, online induction with o1, and the expensive verification process that repeatedly evaluates every proposed rule on 20-25 tasks. Consequently, the paper does not establish lower end-to-end or amortized system cost.

Human evaluation is insufficiently documented: the number and expertise of annotators, blinding, assignment protocol, inter-rater agreement, and uncertainty or significance tests are absent. Several baseline scores are imported from CoSTA* rather than produced under a unified evaluation, making a 0.91 versus 0.94 comparison difficult to interpret.

The evidence for cross-dataset generalization is only a small, selectively displayed set of successful MagicBrush examples. There is no quantitative evaluation, fallback rate, execution cost, or failure analysis on an independent benchmark.

The rule-validation criterion B = delta-cost-percent minus delta-quality-percent is ad hoc, ignores statistical uncertainty, and imposes an unexplained equal trade-off between relative cost and quality changes. Repeated proposal refinement on small samples from a finite image pool further risks validation overfitting.

Reproducibility is weak. Activation conditions such as 'not too small,' 'not too big,' and 'complex scene' lack operational thresholds; the VLM and quality threshold are not clearly specified; model/tool versions, hyperparameters, seeds, and complete timing methodology are missing; and no usable code or project link is provided.

The method is conceptually incremental over CoSTA*: it mines and caches frequent successful paths and falls back to the existing search procedure. The paper does not convincingly distinguish this from experience replay, case-based planning, macro-actions, or straightforward memoization through appropriate baselines.

Important algorithmic details are inconsistent or underspecified. The text says a single minimum-score subroutine is selected when several rules apply, whereas the supplied prompt returns all applicable subroutines without defining the final choice. Algorithm 4 also assigns an undefined x_out after local search. These gaps prevent faithful reimplementation.

The manuscript contains notable presentation and editing problems, including a blank 'Project:' field, duplicate references to CoSTA*, numerous grammatical errors, and an unrelated phrase about 'Bi-Directional Block Self-Attention' inserted into the planning description. Overall, the idea is promising but the current evidence does not support acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The fast-slow approach is intuitive and practically relevant: it reuses validated tool-call subroutines for common image-editing operations while retaining localized A* search as a robust fallback.
The system is described in reasonable detail, including its rule table, algorithms, prompts, trace structure, and subroutine-verification process.

On the reported 121-task, 550-manipulation benchmark, FaSTA* preserves high human-rated quality while materially reducing per-task runtime. The fast-only, slow-only, and verification ablations support the value of its main components.
The paper evaluates different task complexities and text-plus-image cases, and provides reuse, fallback, cost-quality, and qualitative analyses.
weaknesses: The headline 49.3% saving compares FaSTA* at 29.5 seconds with the original 58.2-second CoSTA* configuration. Appendix E shows that the authors' single-chain prompting alone reduces CoSTA* to 46.8 seconds, making the matched improvement attributable to FaSTA* approximately 37%. The main presentation conflates these gains.

Efficiency accounting does not clearly include or amortize expensive learning overhead: OpenAI o1 induction, repeated baseline/candidate evaluations on 20-25 tasks per proposed rule, retries, GPT-4o selection, and additional LLM/VLM queries. The central claim of overall computational efficiency is therefore incomplete.

There is potential evaluation leakage because rules are repeatedly verified using datasets constructed from the same 121 base images used in the final benchmark. Changed prompts reduce direct duplication but do not establish image-level generalization. The MagicBrush evaluation consists only of selected qualitative examples.

The human evaluation omits the number and recruitment of raters, blinding, inter-rater agreement, adjudication, uncertainty estimates, and significance testing. Several baseline results are imported from CoSTA* rather than reproduced in a single controlled evaluation.

The experiment appears to use single runs and provides no confidence intervals or sensitivity analysis for task order, random validation samples, LLM stochasticity, update frequency, quality thresholds, or experience volume. The claimed exponential improvement trend is consequently under-supported.

Reproducibility is limited: the external learning tasks and traces are insufficiently specified, exact LLM/VLM versions and decoding settings are missing, timing boundaries and tool configurations are unclear, and qualitative conditions such as 'not too small' depend on undocumented model judgments.

The contribution is useful but incremental over CoSTA*. Most learned subroutines are familiar detector-segmenter-inpainter pipelines, while the characterization as a novel form of in-context reinforcement learning is stronger than the presented trace summarization and rule filtering justify.

The manuscript contains consistency and clarity issues, including an unrelated phrase inserted in Section 4.3, duplicate references, and overly strong claims about optimal or verifiable A* paths under stochastic tools and a nonstandard objective. Overall, the idea is promising, but stronger leakage-free evaluation and complete cost accounting are needed for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important bottleneck in tool-based image editing: repeatedly searching for similar tool sequences. Reusing validated subroutines with an A* fallback is intuitive and potentially useful.

The fast/slow architecture is clearly motivated, preserves a robust fallback for unfamiliar cases, and is accompanied by useful component ablations, learning-trajectory results, and a complete learned rule table.

The reported controlled comparison is promising: FaSTA* attains 0.91 quality at 29.5 seconds versus 0.93 at 46.8 seconds for the single-chain CoSTA* variant. Results also suggest improvement with additional experience.
The paper covers heterogeneous, long-horizon image-and-text editing tasks and provides qualitative examples, failure categories, prompts, and algorithmic pseudocode.
weaknesses: The evaluation has a serious contamination concern. Proposed rules are verified on datasets constructed from the same 121 base images used in the main CoSTA* benchmark, and accepted or rejected according to performance on those images. Evaluating the resulting rule table on that benchmark does not establish held-out generalization, despite induction traces being sourced externally. A fully disjoint induction/validation/test split is needed.

The headline 49.3% cost reduction conflates two changes and uses the original 58.2-second CoSTA* result. The paper itself shows that changing CoSTA* from a subtask tree to a single chain reduces its cost to 46.8 seconds; against this controlled baseline, the reduction to 29.5 seconds is about 37%, not 49.3%.

The experimental reporting is insufficiently rigorous. Human evaluation omits the number and qualifications of evaluators, blinding and randomization procedures, agreement statistics beyond an unexplained variance, and confidence intervals or significance tests. The size and selection protocol of the reported Complex-Edit subset are also absent.

Efficiency is measured primarily by wall-clock time on one setup, while the method depends on GPT-4o/o1 calls, VLM checks, and periodically repeated validation runs. API latency and monetary/token costs are not clearly incorporated, and the amortization calculation is asserted without enough underlying measurements. This weakens the central efficiency claim.

Novelty is moderate and highly dependent on CoSTA*: the principal addition is LLM-induced conditional reuse of previously successful paths with fallback to the existing search. The only reuse baseline is an unusually brittle exact cache with a fixed 5% tolerance; comparisons to learned retrieval, nearest-neighbor/case-based planning, contextual bandits, policy learning, or program/subroutine induction baselines are missing.

Several results are not reproducible from the manuscript: sampling seeds, exact learning/validation task partitions, quality-check model and threshold details, rule-update histories, full runtime accounting, and repeated-run variability are missing. Closed proprietary LLM dependencies further exacerbate this issue.

Claims such as a “superior Pareto frontier,” generalization, and no compromised output quality are stronger than the evidence: most comparisons reuse numbers from prior work, external-dataset evidence is limited or based on an unspecified subset, and reported quality does decrease from CoSTA*.

strengths: The core idea—mining reusable tool-call subroutines and retaining local A* search as a fallback—is intuitive, practically relevant, and reasonably interpretable.
The manuscript provides prompts, pseudocode, a learned rule table, failure categories, and ablations of verification and fallback mechanisms.
Reported results suggest a potentially useful efficiency–quality trade-off, including lower execution time with only a modest average quality decrease.

weaknesses: The evaluation has serious leakage concerns: rule proposals are repeatedly accepted or rejected using datasets constructed from the same 121 benchmark images later used for the main evaluation. Different prompts do not make this a clean held-out test, especially when activation rules depend directly on image context.

The headline 49.3% saving appears to compare against the original 58.2-second CoSTA* result, although Appendix F shows that the authors’ single-chain modification alone reduces CoSTA* to 46.8 seconds. Against that matched variant, the gain is substantially smaller, making the main comparison potentially misleading.

Most baseline results are imported from the CoSTA* paper rather than obtained through controlled reruns. It is unclear whether hardware, prompts, tool versions, retries, timing boundaries, and available tools are matched. No uncertainty or repeated-run statistics are reported for runtime.

Human evaluation is insufficiently documented: the number and recruitment of raters, blinding, assignment protocol, adjudication, and confidence intervals or significance tests are absent. The stated evaluator variance of 0.07 is not adequately defined.

The Complex-Edit experiment is only on an unspecified subset, with no subset size or selection protocol. MagicBrush evidence is cherry-picked qualitative examples, while the end-to-end model comparison also lacks a reproducible protocol.

The direct-cache baseline uses an arbitrary 5% exact-feature tolerance and is a weak straw man. More meaningful alternatives—retrieval-based reuse, contextual bandits, learned routing, nearest-neighbor policies, and LLM selection without induced symbolic rules—are missing.

The proposed induction is largely prompt-based qualitative bucketing followed by validation, with no principled treatment of noisy correlations, rule uncertainty, multiple testing, distribution drift, or catastrophic rule updates. Calling this in-context reinforcement learning is not technically well justified.

The system uses GPT-4o/o1 calls and additional feature-extraction and verification procedures, yet the principal cost metric is execution time and the accounting of LLM, VLM, induction, and validation overhead is incomplete and mostly supported by an informal amortization argument.

Reproducibility remains limited: exact model/tool versions, thresholds, decoding settings, generated training and verification prompts, random seeds, benchmark subset details, and complete timing methodology are missing.

The presentation contains numerous errors and inconsistencies, including K=20 versus reporting at 40-task intervals, contradictory claims of no quality degradation despite reported degradation, incorrect figure references, and the unrelated phrase “Bi-Directional Block Self-Attention for Fast and Memory-Efficient Sequence Modeling” inserted into the method description. These reduce confidence in the paper’s technical care.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful practical bottleneck in tool-based image editing: repeated A* exploration of tool sequences that have already proved effective in similar contexts.

FaSTA* has an intuitive and useful design, combining interpretable subroutine rules with a conservative localized-search fallback. The fallback makes the efficiency optimization less likely to cause catastrophic task failures.
The manuscript provides extensive methodological detail, including the learned rule table, algorithms, prompts, trace representation, failure categories, and several component ablations.

Reported results are promising: FaSTA* retains human-evaluated quality close to CoSTA* while substantially reducing execution time, and the learning trajectory and 9% fallback rate support the intended mechanism.
The evaluation covers long multi-operation instructions, text-and-image tasks, restricted-tool comparisons, qualitative examples, and an additional Complex-Edit benchmark.
weaknesses: The evaluation has consequential test-set contamination. Subroutine proposals are verified using newly generated prompts on the same 121 base images as the primary CoSTA* benchmark, and the benchmark is repeatedly monitored throughout learning. Thus, the final rule library is not fully independent of the test images, despite the paper's held-out/generalization language.

The independent evidence is insufficient to resolve this concern. Complex-Edit is evaluated only on an unspecified subset, without its size, sampling procedure, confidence intervals, or statistical tests; MagicBrush generalization consists of selected qualitative examples.

The human evaluation protocol omits essential information such as the number and qualifications of evaluators, blinding and randomization, annotation allocation, agreement statistics beyond an unexplained variance value, and uncertainty estimates. Consequently, it is unclear whether the 0.91 versus 0.94 quality difference is reliably small.

Cost accounting is inconsistent or insufficiently documented. The claimed 49.3% reduction does not transparently follow from some reported figures—for example, 46.8 to 29.5 seconds is about 37%—and LLM/VLM calls, failed fast-path work, rule induction, and verification are not fully incorporated into a reproducible end-to-end cost analysis. The amortized-over-2,000-tasks calculation is asserted with limited derivation.

Most comparisons outside CoSTA* reuse values from the earlier paper rather than rerunning all methods under a unified environment. The restricted-tool experiments help, but their sharply different absolute scores and limited protocol description make them difficult to reconcile with the main results.

The direct-cache baseline is unusually restrictive, requiring context features to fall within a 5% tolerance, and stronger alternatives are missing: nearest-neighbor retrieval over traces, semantic retrieval with demonstrations, frequency-based subroutines without LLM induction, or learned routing/classification.

The novelty is moderate: the central mechanism is experience compression into conditional macros followed by search fallback. The paper does not rigorously isolate whether gains arise from LLM-based induction, manual feature design, repeated validation on benchmark-distribution images, or simply caching common toolpaths.

Several reproducibility details remain unclear, including exact dataset splits and task counts, model/tool versions and inference settings, quality thresholds, random seeds, API settings and monetary costs, and the construction and sampling of external learning data. The manuscript's code link is also not concretely accessible in the submitted text.

There are internal clarity and correctness issues, including inconsistent update intervals (K=20 versus learning points at 40-task intervals), an unrelated phrase inserted into the activation-rule description, and claims such as 'no degradation of final quality' that conflict with the reported decline from 0.93 to 0.91.
